issues.legal_issue: A specific direction on remand to assess land required for firewood purposes governs the subsequent determination and cannot be displaced by applying an inconsistent rule from another case.
material_facts: The Supreme Court had remanded the matter with a direction to determine the extent of land required for growing firewood for the plantations’ factories and employees.
The High Court later relied on another decision to deny exemption for forest land unless it was proved to have been actually used for firewood in 1971.
The Supreme Court held that the other decision did not apply in light of its specific remand direction.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in relying on the other decision; the specific remand direction governed, without determining the ultimate extent of land qualifying for exemption.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the earlier remand decision in Pioneer Rubber Plantation, Nilambur, Kerala State v. State of Kerala, (1992) 4 SCC 175, which interpreted Section 2(f)(1)(i)(B) of the Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971 to permit exemption for the minimum reasonable area needed to grow firewood for factories or smoke-houses and, where proved, employees’ domestic use, subject to the stated conditions. It held that the later decision in State of Kerala v. Pullengode Rubber Produce Co. Ltd., (1999) 6 SCC 92, had no application after the specific remand direction in this case.

predicates.appeal_after_specific_remand: The matter came before a later court in an appeal after an earlier remand.
predicates.remand_requires_assessment_of_required_l: The earlier remand directed the decision-maker to assess the extent of land required for the stated purpose.
predicates.later_court_applies_inconsistent_actual_: The later court applied a requirement that the land must have been actually used for the purpose at the relevant time.

issues.definition: When an appeal follows a specific remand requiring an assessment of land needed for a stated purpose, a later court’s inconsistent actual-use test does not displace that remand direction.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court must decide on its merits an application to produce additional evidence, applying the statutory conditions for admission and giving reasons when evidence is admitted.
material_facts: Both sides filed applications in the High Court appeal seeking to produce additional materials.
The High Court referred to the applications but did not decide them.
The Supreme Court declined to assess the materials itself and directed the High Court to decide the applications and then dispose of the appeal.

The Supreme Court stated that additional evidence may be received where evidence was wrongly refused below, could not despite due diligence have been produced earlier, or is required to enable judgment or for another substantial cause; it may not be used to fill gaps or patch weak points.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was required to decide the additional-evidence applications on their merits; the applications were left for the High Court to determine under the applicable legal standard.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure limits the production of additional evidence in an appeal to specified circumstances and requires the appellate court to record reasons when it allows such evidence. Additional evidence cannot be used to fill lacunae or patch weak points. The Court relied on Jatinder Singh v. Mehar Singh, AIR 2009 SC 354, and Shyam Gopal Bindal v. Land Acquisition Officer, (2010) 2 SCC 316.

predicates.appeal_from_original_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from an original decree.
predicates.additional_evidence_application_filed: A party has applied in the appeal to produce additional evidence.

issues.definition: When an additional-evidence application is filed in an appeal from an original decree, the appellate court must decide that application on its merits.
